title: Hubble image of galaxy cluster MACS J1206
caption: The galaxy cluster MACS J1206, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: MACS J1206.2-0847 · constellation Virgo · about 4 billion light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, M. Postman (STScI) and the CLASH Team

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble picture shows the galaxy cluster MACS J1206, which lies about 4 billion light-years away. Clusters like this one are worth studying for several reasons.

A galaxy cluster holds an enormous amount of mass, and its gravity is strong enough to bend the path of light visibly, a little like a magnifying glass. That makes clusters useful tools. They amplify the light of distant galaxies behind them, bringing faraway objects within reach.

The lensed images carry information too. Their exact shapes hold clues about spacetime, about how the Universe expands and about how dark matter is spread through the cluster. MACS J1206 is one of 25 clusters studied in the CLASH program, short for Cluster Lensing and Supernova survey with Hubble. The project is assembling a large collection of scientific data on lensing clusters for astronomers to use.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.78 x 2.52 arcminutes) and distance (4 billion light years), the frame spans roughly 3.2 million × 2.9 million light-years. Its light set out about 4,000 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed MACS J1206 in visible and near-infrared light. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Much of this light is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and a cluster this far away is far too faint for any unaided eye.
